title: Source Degeneration
intro: A resistor in the source of a CS device trades gain for linearity and raises the output resistance. The analysis also yields the most useful shortcut in the chapter, $A_v = -G_m R_{out}$ (Razavi, Section 3.3.6).

blocks.alt: Common-source stage: NMOS M1 with gate driven by Vin, drain connected through RD to VDD with the output Vout taken at the drain, and a resistor RS from the source to ground.
blocks.caption: CS stage with source degeneration.

blocks.text: When $V_{in}$ rises, the drain current and the drop across $R_S$ rise too, so only part of the input change reaches $V_{GS}$. Define the stage's transconductance $G_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{in}$. With $V_{GS} = V_{in} - I_D R_S$ and $\lambda = \gamma = 0$:

blocks.tex: G_m = \frac{g_m}{1 + g_m R_S}, \qquad A_v = -G_m R_D = -\frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S} = -\frac{R_D}{\frac{1}{g_m} + R_S}

blocks.text: For $R_S \gg 1/g_m$, $G_m \approx 1/R_S$: almost all of the input change appears across the resistor and $\Delta I_D \approx \Delta V_{in}/R_S$, so the current is a linearized function of the input. The price is lower gain (and, as shown under Noise, more noise).

blocks.alt: Plot of transconductance in millisiemens against input voltage from 0.3 to 1.5 volts. A dashed line, the plain transistor's gm, rises linearly from zero at 0.4 volts to above 3 mS. The solid curve with 1 kilohm degeneration starts the same way but bends over and flattens toward a dotted horizontal line at 1 mS, the value of 1 over RS.
blocks.caption: Gm with and without degeneration. Near threshold the two agree; at high overdrive Gm saturates at 1/RS, which makes the gain nearly constant.

blocks.text: In large-signal terms: near threshold $1/g_m \gg R_S$ and the stage behaves as if undegenerated; as the overdrive grows $g_m R_S$ takes over and $G_m$ approaches $1/R_S$. The gain therefore starts at about $-g_m R_D$, becomes $-g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S)$ and levels off near $-R_D/R_S$, until the drain drops low enough ($R_D I_D > V_{DD} - V_{in} + V_{TH}$) to push M1 into triode.

The last form of the gain reads naturally: $|A_v|$ equals the resistance seen at the drain divided by the resistance in the source path, where the source path is $1/g_m$ (looking into the source) plus whatever explicit resistance is there. For example, a diode-connected device M2 in the source of M1 gives $A_v = -R_D/(1/g_{m1} + 1/g_{m2})$.

Apply $v_X$ to the drain (without $R_D$) and include body effect. The current $i_X$ flows through $R_S$, so $v_{gs} = v_{bs} = -i_X R_S$; the current through $r_o$ is $i_X + (g_m + g_{mb})R_S i_X$. Adding the drops across $r_o$ and $R_S$:

Two views of the same result: $r_o$ boosted by $1 + (g_m + g_{mb})R_S$ and added to $R_S$, or $R_S$ boosted by about the intrinsic gain and added to $r_o$. Physically, raising the drain pushes more current through $R_S$, which lowers $V_{GS}$ (and raises $V_{TH}$) and opposes the current increase. A third derivation: the source of M1 sees $1/(g_m + g_{mb})$ upward, which in parallel with $R_S$ forms a divider with $r_o$, so only a small fraction of the drain change reaches the source. The stage's total output resistance is $R_{out} \parallel R_D$.
The general gain and the gain lemma
With $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ included, the degenerated device's transconductance and the full gain are

blocks.tex: A_v = \frac{-g_m r_o R_D}{R_D + R_S + r_o + (g_m + g_{mb})R_S r_o}

blocks.text: The gain factors into exactly that $G_m$ times the parallel combination of $R_D$ with the $R_{out}$ above. This is no coincidence. Any linear circuit's output looks like a Norton equivalent, a current source $G_m v_{in}$ in parallel with $R_{out}$, so

blocks.caption: Gain lemma: $G_m$ from the output current with the output shorted to AC ground; $R_{out}$ with the input set to zero

blocks.text: It is often far easier to find $G_m$ and $R_{out}$ by inspection than to solve the whole circuit. Example: bias a degenerated device with an ideal current source as the load. Then $R_{out}$ is the boosted expression above and $G_m$ is its reciprocal times $g_m r_o$, so $A_v = -g_m r_o$, independent of $R_S$. Intuitively, an ideal current source allows no signal current through $R_S$, so $R_S$ carries no signal voltage and might as well be absent.

blocks.title: Degeneration trades gain for linearity
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ ($r_o$ infinite). Find the gain for $R_S = 500\,\Omega$ and for $R_S = 5\text{ k}\Omega$.

blocks.title: Gm and Rout with everything included
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{mb} = 0.4\text{ mS}$, $r_o = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_S = 1\text{ k}\Omega$, $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$. Find $G_m$, $R_{out}$ (excluding $R_D$) and the gain.
solution: $(g_m + g_{mb})R_S = 2.4$. $G_m = \frac{40}{1\text{ k}\Omega + 3.4 \cdot 20\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{40}{69\text{ k}\Omega} \approx 0.58\text{ mS}$ (the simple formula gives 0.67 mS).
$A_v = -G_m(R_{out} \parallel R_D) = -0.58\text{ mS} \cdot 8.73\text{ k}\Omega \approx -5.06$. The full formula agrees: $-400\text{ k}\Omega/(10 + 1 + 20 + 48)\text{ k}\Omega = -5.06$.

blocks.title: A diode in the source
blocks.text: M1 ($g_{m1} = 2\text{ mS}$) has a diode-connected M2 ($g_{m2} = 1\text{ mS}$) in its source and $R_D = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ in its drain. Ignoring $\lambda$ and $\gamma$, find the gain.

blocks.title: Degeneration with a current-source load
blocks.text: A degenerated device with $g_m r_o = 40$ and $R_S = 2\text{ k}\Omega$ drives an ideal current-source load. Find the gain. What changes if $R_S$ is doubled?
solution: Nothing: the ideal source forces zero signal current through $R_S$, so its value does not matter.
